tierWindow.goal: Produce the core research-document genres - the literature review, the research proposal and the report - so that each does the work its reader expects.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Application and analysis (structure, shape, distinguish, produce); recognising and correcting genre errors in worked examples, not only naming them.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Whole genres with several coordinated parts; conventions that must be held together, such as keeping results apart from discussion, or narrowing a topic to a researchable focus.
tierWindow.autonomy: Moderate scaffolding; worked contrasts and checklists; the learner is expected to carry each convention into their own subject rather than be walked through it.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner already knows what research is and how a project is shaped (the introductory tier) and can read sources critically. They have met the literature review, the proposal and the report as genres that exist, but have not yet produced them to convention. Teach the genres as documents to make well, not as ideas to recognise.

subThemes.label: A literature review critiques the discourse; it is not a description of who said what, when
Analysis, evaluation and synthesis as the moves that make a literature review a critique

Freshness of perspective rather than total originality as what a proposal must show
The core elements of a report: introduction, methodology, results and discussion
Keeping results (what was found) apart from discussion (what it means)

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons, one per genre. First, the literature review: how it critiques the discourse rather than listing who said what. Second, the research proposal: how a framework of questions narrows a topic and shows its freshness. Third, the report: how its core elements are organised, and why results and discussion stay apart. Work through them in order.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about the documents that carry research: the literature review, the research proposal and the report. Each is a genre with its own job and its own conventions, and the work here is producing them well. By the end you will be able to explain how a literature review critiques the discourse, shape a proposal as a framework of questions, and structure a report so its core elements do their work.

These genres are where a research project becomes visible to others. A marker, a supervisor or a funding panel reads your review, proposal or report and judges the work through it. Knowing what each genre is for, and writing to that purpose, is what turns sound research into work that is recognised and trusted.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain how a literature review critiques the discourse, shape a proposal as a framework of questions, structure a report so its core elements do their work.

practiceConnection.academic: These genres are the working documents of research in every discipline. A literature review opens a dissertation or an article; a proposal wins approval or funding for a project; a report communicates what was done and what was found. Produce them well now and you are equipped for the research your degree, and much professional work, will ask of you.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced Researching and Research Methods course takes you into running research with rigour and ethics, from consent and data handling to the principles of research integrity. Going wider: Academic Writing and Criticality sharpen the writing and judgement that every one of these genres depends on.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. The three documents that carry research are no longer just genres you read, but genres you can produce. You can write a literature review that critiques the discourse rather than listing sources. You can shape a proposal as a framework of questions that narrows a topic and shows its freshness. And you can structure a report so its core elements each do their work, with results and discussion kept apart. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, these genres are the working documents of your research. A dissertation opens with a literature review; a funded project begins as a proposal; findings are communicated as a report. Each time you write one to its purpose, rather than merely to its format, you are doing the work that research degrees and research careers are built on.
